power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: Study STEP2
table.research_questions:
Aim 1: To better understand the different dimensions assessed by various measures related to self-transcendent experiences, emotions and mystical experiences, and to enhance conceptual understanding of what the facets of mystical/self-transcendent experiences are in relation to psychedelics, we will conduct an exploratory factor analysis of: Piff’s small self-scale (small self size, vastness relative to self items), Yaden’s self-transcendent experiences scale (self-loss and connection self-transcendent experiences subscales), the mystical experiences questionnaire (transcendence of time and space, ineffability, positive mood, mystical experiences subscales), self-transcendent emotions from the modified differential emotions scale, and the inclusion of self in other scale. Given the exploratory nature of the analysis, we have no a priori hypothesis. However, we will explore whether factors map onto theorized dimensions of self-transcendence (self-loss and connection self-transcendent experiences, self-transcendent emotions distinct from positive emotions). 

Aim 2–5: Examine the extent to which the resulting factors are associated with: (a) negative emotions during the substance experience [Aim 2]; (b) persisting positive effects [Aim 3], as well as (c) set [Aim 4] and (d) setting variables [Aim 5]. Because the factors emerging from the exploratory factor analysis are unknown, we do not specify a priori hypotheses.
table.study_type: Observational Study - Data is collected from study subjects that are not randomly assigned to a treatment. This includes surveys, “natural experiments,” and regression discontinuity designs.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.existing_data: Registration following analysis of the data

table.measured_variables:
Participants completed the below measures in reference to a cannabis, psilocybin or MDMA use experience of at least ‘moderate’ intensity that occurred during the past 5 years. 

Primary purpose for use: “What was your main purpose for using [cannabis/psilocybin/MDMA] at this time?” Response options: To have fun, for enjoyment, or to celebrate, To treat a mental or physical health condition, To improve or change myself (self-optimization or self-change),For spiritual reasons, To participate in a ceremonial event, Curiosity, To deepen a connection with others, earth, or nature, Distract myself/escape from my problems, To enhance sex, For another reason.

Spiritual motivations. This 5-item self-report survey inquired about the strength of spiritual or prosocial motivations for substance use (sample item: “I wanted greater capacity to love all beings”). Responses are made on a Likert scale ranging from 1 (Not at all important) to 6 (Very important). 

Intentions and mindset: Participants were asked questions about their mindset as they took the drug [MDMA/psilocybin/cannabis]. Two items assessed clarity of intentions (sample item: “I have a clear intention for the upcoming experience”), adapted from a prior study (Haijen et al., 2018). Four items were selected from a state of surrender subscale (Russ et al., 2019). A single-item adapted from (Russ et al., 2019) inquired about apprehension felt immediately before taking psilocybin/MDMA/cannabis.  Responses were made on a Likert scale ranging from 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 4 (Strongly Agree).

Self-Transcendent Experiences. This nine item self-report survey assessed the degree to which individuals have experienced “self-loss” and “connection” self-transcendent experiences with MDMA/psilocybin/cannabis (Yaden, 2020). Responses are made on a Likert scale ranging from 0 (Not at all) to 4 (Extremely).

Mystical Experiences Questionnaire. This 30-item self-report survey (Barrett et al., 2015) measured various facets of mystical experiences: transcendence of time and space (sample item: “Loss of your usual sense of time”), ineffability (sample item: “Sense that the experience cannot be described adequately in words”), positive mood (sample item: “Experience of ecstasy”), and overall mystical experiences (sample item: “Experience of the fusion of your personal self into a larger whole”). Responses were made on a Likert scale ranging from 0 (None/not at all) to (5) Extreme (more than any other time in my life and stronger than 4).

Self-Transcendent Emotions: Five items adapted from the modified Differential Emotion Scale (Fredrickson et al., 2003) were selected to assess awe (“awe, wonder, or amazement”), gratitude (“grateful, appreciative, or thankful”), inspiration (“inspired, uplifted, or elevated”), love (“love, closeness, or trust”), and sympathy (“sympathy, concern, or compassion”). Participants rated the peak intensity of each emotion during their experience on a Likert scale ranging from 0 (Not at all) to 4 (Extremely).

Small Self Scale: Participants responded to four items adapted from  (Piff et al., 2015), three assessing vastness relative to the self (sample item: “I felt the presence of something greater than myself”) and one assessing self-diminishment (sample item: “I felt small or insignificant”). Responses were made on a Likert scale ranging from 1 (Not at all True) to 7 (Very True). 

Self-Other Overlap: The single-item Inclusion of Other in the Self Scale includes a series of ven diagrams depicting overlap between self/others with increasing overlap. Responses range from 1 (no overlap) to 7 (mostly overlapping), with a N/A (I was not with others) option available. 

Positive and Negative Emotions: The 10-item International Positive and Negative Affect Schedule – Short Form (Thompson, 2007) was used to assess overall positive emotions and negative emotions during their substance use experience. Responses were made on a Likert scale ranging from 1 (Very slightly or not at all) to 5 (Extremely).

Persisting Positive Effects. Participants indicated the extent to which they believed the experience and their contemplation of that experience led to long-term and persisting changes in: their current sense of personal well-being or life satisfaction, the sense of their life's purpose, their mood; and behavioral changes. Responses were made on a scale ranging from –3 (Strong negative change that I consider undesirable) to +3 (Strong positive change that I consider desirable) with 0 indicating ‘No Change’.
table.indices:
Primary purpose for use: Responses are coded into a binary variable capturing whether use was healing/growth-oriented (i.e., treating a mental or physical health condition, self-improvement, spiritual reasons or deepening a connection) versus non-healing/growth oriented (i.e., reactional or distraction purposes).

Spiritual motivations. Items are averaged into a composite spiritual/prosocial motivation score.

Intentions and mindset: Items assessed clarity of intentions are averaged together. Items assessing state of surrender subscale are averaged together. The single item assessing apprehension is kept separate. 

Self-Transcendent Experiences. Items are averaged into a self-loss self-transcendent experience and connection self-transcendent experience subscale. 

Mystical Experiences Questionnaire. Items are averaged into a total MEQ score and subscales: transcendence of time and space, ineffability, positive mood, and mystical experiences. Per convention (Griffiths et al., 2018), subscale and total scores were calculated as a percentage of the maximum possible score, and thus could range from 0–100.  

Self-Transcendent Emotions: Items are averaged into a composite self-transcendent emotion score. 

Small Self Scale: The three items assessing vastness relative to the self will be averaged, and the item assessing self-diminishment kept separate.  

Self-Other Overlap: N/A – single item measure.  

Positive and Negative Emotions: Items are averaged into a positive emotions and negative emotions subscale.

Persisting Positive Effects. Items will be averaged into an overall persisting positive effects subscale. Scores will be converted to percentage of maximum score as performed in previous analyses (Griffiths et al., 2011, 2016).
table.statistical_tests:
Aim 1: To better understand the different dimensions assessed by various measures related to self-transcendent experiences, emotions and mystical experiences, and to enhance conceptual understanding of what the facets of mystical/self-transcendent experiences are in relation to psychedelics, we will conduct an exploratory factor analysis of: Piff’s small self-scale (small self size, vastness relative to self items), Yaden’s self-transcendent experiences scale (self-loss and connection self-transcendent experiences subscales), the mystical experiences questionnaire (transcendence of time and space, ineffability, positive mood, mystical experiences subscales), the self-transcendent emotions from the modified differential emotions scale, and the inclusion of self in other scale. 

Corresponding Aim 1 Analytic Approach: Prior to running analyses, correlations between measures will be examined. Because measures were administered on distinct scales, all variables will be z-score standardized to ensure comparability before conducting the exploratory factor analysis (EFA). Best practices for EFA are followed based upon (Goretzko et al., 2021). Prior to running the EFA, assumptions will be tested— histograms will be used to inspect for extreme outliers, multivariate normality will be assessed via diagnostic plot examination (scatter plots, Mahalanobis Distance Q-Q plot). Multicollinearity will be assessed via inspecting inter-measure correlations. Factorability of the data will be assessed using the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure and Bartlett’s test of sphericity to ensure correlations are sufficient for factor analysis. A maximum likelihood EFA will be used unless multivariate normality is significantly violated, in which case a Weighted Least Squares Mean and Variance adjusted (WLSMV) factoring approach will be used. 

Based on the assumption that several measures will be at least moderately intercorrelated, an oblique rotation will be used—factor analysis pattern results with promax and oblimin rotations will be compared, with the final model selected based upon theoretical parsimony. To determine the number of factors to retain in the exploratory factor analysis, we will use a combination of empirical, descriptive and theoretical criteria. First, we will conduct Parallel Analysis (PA) and Comparison Data (CD) procedures. Second, we will consider item-level communalities and factor loadings. Third, we will incorporate theoretical interpretability, including that items with weak communalities or problematic cross-loadings will be considered for removal. Factor analysis with full items and with removed items will be compared using by interpretability and stability of factor structure, and the model with the best theoretical fit and parsimony. 

Aim 2–5: Examine the extent to which the factors identified in Aim 1 are associated with: (1) negative emotions during the substance experience [Aim 2]; (2) persisting positive effects [Aim 3], as well as (3) set [Aim 4] and (4) setting variables [Aim 5]. Because the factors emerging from the exploratory factor analysis are unknown, we do not specify a priori hypotheses. 

Corresponding Aim 2–5 analytic approach: Individual regression-based factor scores will be calculated (McNeish & Wolf, 2020). Prior to running regressions, we will examine zero-order correlations between factors and study variables. We will conduct a series of hierarchical multiple linear regression. Prior to conducting linear regressions, assumptions will be checked by visual inspection of diagnostic plots and by calculating variance inflation factor values. Robust standard errors will be used if heteroscedasticity is observed. Non-parametric alternates (generalized linear models) will be used if the assumption of normality of residuals is violated. The generalized linear model will be selected based upon model fit, assessed via inspection of residual and Q-Q plots. If multicollinearity is observed, single predictors will be used in lieu of multivariate models. For binary outcomes (healing/growth-oriented motivations), we will use binomial logistic regression. 

We will test the following models:
- Model 1: All factors (determined via the Aim 1 EFA) together predicting negative emotion, as assessed by the PANAS
- Model 2: All factors together predicting positive persisting effects
- Model 3: All factors together predicting state of surrender 
- Model 4: All factors together predicting apprehensiveness
- Model 5: All factors together predicting clear intentions
- Model 6: All factors together predicting spiritual/prosocial motivations
- Model 7: All factors together predicting primary purpose for use (healing/growth-oriented motivations (yes/no))
table.inference_criteria: Inferences will primarily be based on effect sizes—correlation coefficients for bivariate associations and regression coefficients (β or their GLM equivalents) for multivariable models. An alpha level of .05 will be used to assess statistical significance.

Spiritual motivations. This 5-item self-report survey inquired about the strength of spiritual or prosocial motivations for substance use (sample item: “I wanted greater capacity to love all beings”). Responses are made on a Likert scale ranging from 1 (Not at all important) to 6 (Very important).

Intentions and mindset: Participants were asked questions about their mindset as they took the drug [MDMA/psilocybin/cannabis]. Self-Transcendent Experiences. This nine item self-report survey assessed the degree to which individuals have experienced “self-loss” and “connection” self-transcendent experiences with MDMA/psilocybin/cannabis (Yaden, 2020). Responses are made on a Likert scale ranging from 0 (Not at all) to 4 (Extremely).

Self-Transcendent Emotions: Five items adapted from the modified Differential Emotion Scale (Fredrickson et al., 2003) were selected to assess awe (“awe, wonder, or amazement”), gratitude (“grateful, appreciative, or thankful”), inspiration (“inspired, uplifted, or elevated”), love (“love, closeness, or trust”), and sympathy (“sympathy, concern, or compassion”). Participants rated the peak intensity of each emotion during their experience on a Likert scale ranging from 0 (Not at all) to 4 (Extremely).

Small Self Scale: Participants responded to four items adapted from (Piff et al., 2015), three assessing vastness relative to the self (sample item: “I felt the presence of something greater than myself”) and one assessing self-diminishment (sample item: “I felt small or insignificant”). Responses were made on a Likert scale ranging from 1 (Not at all True) to 7 (Very True).

Self-Other Overlap: The single-item Inclusion of Other in the Self Scale includes a series of ven diagrams depicting overlap between self/others with increasing overlap. Responses range from 1 (no overlap) to 7 (mostly overlapping), with a N/A (I was not with others) option available.

Positive and Negative Emotions: The 10-item International Positive and Negative Affect Schedule – Short Form (Thompson, 2007) was used to assess overall positive emotions and negative emotions during their substance use experience. Responses were made on a Likert scale ranging from 1 (Very slightly or not at all) to 5 (Extremely).

Persisting Positive Effects. Participants indicated the extent to which they believed the experience and their contemplation of that experience led to long-term and persisting changes in: their current sense of personal well-being or life satisfaction, the sense of their life's purpose, their mood; and behavioral changes. Corresponding Aim 1 Analytic Approach: Prior to running analyses, correlations between measures will be examined. Because measures were administered on distinct scales, all variables will be z-score standardized to ensure comparability before conducting the exploratory factor analysis (EFA). Best practices for EFA are followed based upon (Goretzko et al., 2021). Prior to running the EFA, assumptions will be tested— histograms will be used to inspect for extreme outliers, multivariate normality will be assessed via diagnostic plot examination (scatter plots, Mahalanobis Distance Q-Q plot). Multicollinearity will be assessed via inspecting inter-measure correlations. Factorability of the data will be assessed using the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure and Bartlett’s test of sphericity to ensure correlations are sufficient for factor analysis. A maximum likelihood EFA will be used unless multivariate normality is significantly violated, in which case a Weighted Least Squares Mean and Variance adjusted (WLSMV) factoring approach will be used.

Based on the assumption that several measures will be at least moderately intercorrelated, an oblique rotation will be used—factor analysis pattern results with promax and oblimin rotations will be compared, with the final model selected based upon theoretical parsimony. To determine the number of factors to retain in the exploratory factor analysis, we will use a combination of empirical, descriptive and theoretical criteria. First, we will conduct Parallel Analysis (PA) and Comparison Data (CD) procedures. Second, we will consider item-level communalities and factor loadings. Third, we will incorporate theoretical interpretability, including that items with weak communalities or problematic cross-loadings will be considered for removal. Factor analysis with full items and with removed items will be compared using by interpretability and stability of factor structure, and the model with the best theoretical fit and parsimony.

Aim 2–5: Examine the extent to which the factors identified in Aim 1 are associated with: (1) negative emotions during the substance experience [Aim 2]; (2) persisting positive effects [Aim 3], as well as (3) set [Aim 4] and (4) setting variables [Aim 5]. Because the factors emerging from the exploratory factor analysis are unknown, we do not specify a priori hypotheses.

Corresponding Aim 2–5 analytic approach: Individual regression-based factor scores will be calculated (McNeish & Wolf, 2020). Prior to running regressions, we will examine zero-order correlations between factors and study variables. We will conduct a series of hierarchical multiple linear regression. Prior to conducting linear regressions, assumptions will be checked by visual inspection of diagnostic plots and by calculating variance inflation factor values. Robust standard errors will be used if heteroscedasticity is observed. Non-parametric alternates (generalized linear models) will be used if the assumption of normality of residuals is violated. The generalized linear model will be selected based upon model fit, assessed via inspection of residual and Q-Q plots. If multicollinearity is observed, single predictors will be used in lieu of multivariate models. For binary outcomes (healing/growth-oriented motivations), we will use binomial logistic regression.

- Model 4: All factors together predicting apprehensiveness
- Model 5: All factors together predicting clear intentions
- Model 6: All factors together predicting spiritual/prosocial motivations

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------

-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
```

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .46", "p = .10"), Sentence = c("Results from Model 2 indicated that the Connection and Positive Emotions factor score was associated with greater positive persisting effects (B = 6.46, β = .30, SE = 1.50, t = 4.30, 95% CI [3.79, 9.13], p < .001), whereas the Time, Space and Self-Transcendence factor score was not (B = 1.05, β = .05, SE = 1.44, t = 0.73, 95% CI [-1.62, 3.73], p = .46).", "The Connection/Positive Emotion showed a small, statistically significant association with greater clarity of intentions at time of ingestion (B = .17, β = .19, SE = 0.06, t = 2.87, 95% CI [.06, .27], p = .004), whereas this association was small and nonsignificant for the Space/Time/Self-Transcendence factor (B = .10, β = .11, SE = 0.05, t = 1.63, 95% CI [-.01, .21], p = .10)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. ownership.dep_description: Psychedelics frequently occasion mystical and self-transcendent experiences. Delineating different dimensions of such experiences may be important, as they may have distinct associations with beneficial outcomes. Yet, common measures often blend constructs (e.g., general positive affect with self-transcendent ‘other-oriented’ emotions, experiences involving a loss of self or space with those involving feelings of interconnection/unity), potentially overlooking meaningful distinctions in the qualities of self-transcendent experiences arising from psychedelics. Furthermore, psychedelic research often uses psychedelic-specific measures, complicating the establishment of conceptual and empirical links with broader transpersonal, psychological, and affective science literatures. To address these gaps, we propose to integrate psychedelic-specific (MEQ-30) related to self-transcendence with general (non-psychedelic-specific) measures to explore the structure of self-transcendent experience...

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 3 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 3 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:3, File = c("STEP1 analysis syntax_shareable.R", 
"step2_code_shareable.R", "STEP analysis syntax_shareable.R"), 
    "Runs after" = c("—", "—", "—"), Basis = c("numeric", 
    "numeric", "none")), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 3 scripts: 1 ran without error, 2 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. 

*a script hit a `could not find function "..."` error; we added the `library()` calls it needs (see below), and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.*

```{r}

table <- structure(list(File = c("STEP1 analysis syntax_shareable.R", 
"step2_code_shareable.R", "STEP analysis syntax_shareable.R"), 
    Outcome = c("errored", "ran_ok", "errored"), Detail = c("undefined_variable", 
    "", "undefined_variable"), "Time (s)" = c(47.6, 19.5, 43.2
    )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Undefined-variable errors**

**2 scripts failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("STEP1 analysis syntax_shareable.R", 
"STEP analysis syntax_shareable.R"), "Missing variable" = c("ste_selfloss_sum2", 
"ste_selfloss_sum2"), "Defined in" = c("(not defined anywhere in the paper's code)", 
"(not defined anywhere in the paper's code)")), row.names = c(NA, 
-2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**3 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.
Reproducible after removing `setwd()`: step2_code_shareable.R.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("STEP analysis syntax_shareable.R", "STEP1 analysis syntax_shareable.R", 
"step2_code_shareable.R"), "setwd() removed" = c(1L, 1L, 1L), 
    "Path(s) it set" = c("C:/Users/chris/Dropbox/__PPC/STEP 1", 
    "C:/Users/chris/Dropbox/__PPC/STEP 1", "C:/Users/chris/Dropbox/__PPC/___STEP 2 - psychometrics/analyses"
    )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**`library()` calls added**

**2 scripts use functions from packages they do not load themselves.** The packages are usually loaded in another script of the project, which only helps when the scripts run in one R session in the right order. To run them we added the `library()` calls below at the top. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after adding `library()` calls it should make itself**.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("STEP1 analysis syntax_shareable.R", 
"STEP analysis syntax_shareable.R"), "library() calls added" = c("library(dplyr)", 
"library(dplyr)")), row.names = c("STEP1 analysis syntax_shareable.R", 
"STEP analysis syntax_shareable.R"), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```

text.text: The authors would like to thank Will Lucas for his support with survey creation and administration.

Ethics approval and consent to participate: Study procedures were approved by the Behavioral Health Research Collective Institutional Review Board (#047) and carried out in accordance with the provisions of the World Medical Association Declaration of Helsinki.
Written verbal consent was obtained for all participants.
Self-transcendent experiences are a broad class of altered states of consciousness that lack a single, widely accepted definition.

They have been variably described as feeling "connected to something larger than or outside of your everyday sense of self" (Garcia-Romeu et al., 2015), as "transient mental states of decreased self-salience and increased feelings of connectedness" (Yaden et al., 2017a), and as an inherently human orientation toward values, meaning, or causes beyond the self (Frankl, 1966).
text.formatted: They have been variably described as feeling "connected to something larger than or outside of your everyday sense of self" <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Garcia-Romeu et al., 2015)</ref>, as "transient mental states of decreased self-salience and increased feelings of connectedness" <ref type="bibr">(Yaden et al., 2017a)</ref>, and as an inherently human orientation toward values, meaning, or causes beyond the self <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Frankl, 1966)</ref>.

text.text: Self-transcendent experiences are closely related to philosophical and contemplative concepts, such as Thich Nhat Hanh's notion of "interbeing"-the profound interconnectedness and interdependence of all things (Hanh, 2017), as well as spiritual, mystical, religious and sacred experiences (MacLean et al., 2012; Stace, 1960).
text.formatted: Self-transcendent experiences are closely related to philosophical and contemplative concepts, such as Thich Nhat Hanh's notion of "interbeing"-the profound interconnectedness and interdependence of all things <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Hanh, 2017)</ref>, as well as spiritual, mystical, religious and sacred experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(MacLean et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Stace, 1960)</ref>.

text.text: Self-transcendent experiences may also entail deeply felt positive mood (Pahnke, 1963) and self-transcendent emotions (e.g., awe, compassion, gratitude) (Cova & Seragnoli, 2025)-a category of positive emotion that involves attention beyond one's self, such as to the needs of others, thought to have a salient social bonding and altruism function (Gordon et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Self-transcendent experiences may also entail deeply felt positive mood <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Pahnke, 1963)</ref> and self-transcendent emotions (e.g., awe, compassion, gratitude) <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Cova & Seragnoli, 2025)</ref>-a category of positive emotion that involves attention beyond one's self, such as to the needs of others, thought to have a salient social bonding and altruism function <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Gordon et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Self-transcendent experiences are often experienced as profoundly meaningful and transformative (Griffiths et al., 2008) and can elicit a range of downstream intra-and interpersonal benefits (Gordon et al., 2017; Griffiths et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Self-transcendent experiences are often experienced as profoundly meaningful and transformative <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Griffiths et al., 2008)</ref> and can elicit a range of downstream intra-and interpersonal benefits <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Gordon et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Griffiths et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kim et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: They are believed to contribute to wellness and meaning in life (e.g., Frankl, 1966) and are thought to be central to the efficacy of several interventions for wellbeing and mental health, including mindfulness and contemplative practices (Hanley et al., 2020; Verhaeghen, 2019; Wong, 2016).
text.formatted: They are believed to contribute to wellness and meaning in life (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Frankl, 1966)</ref> and are thought to be central to the efficacy of several interventions for wellbeing and mental health, including mindfulness and contemplative practices <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Hanley et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Verhaeghen, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Wong, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In psychedelic-assisted therapies, in particular, self-transcendent and "mystical-type" experiences have been repeatedly implicated as candidate mechanisms of therapeutic change (van Elk & Yaden, 2022; Yaden & Griffiths, 2021).
text.formatted: In psychedelic-assisted therapies, in particular, self-transcendent and "mystical-type" experiences have been repeatedly implicated as candidate mechanisms of therapeutic change <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(van Elk & Yaden, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Yaden & Griffiths, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Psychedelic compounds reliably occasion intense forms of self-transcendent and mystical experiences, regarded as central explanatory constructs in their therapeutic effects (Romeo et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Psychedelic compounds reliably occasion intense forms of self-transcendent and mystical experiences, regarded as central explanatory constructs in their therapeutic effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Romeo et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Psychedelic-assisted therapy research frequently treats mystical and self-transcendent experiences as a holistic phenomenon.

For instance, the Mystical Experience Questionnaire (MEQ30; MacLean et al., 2012)-one of the most commonly used measures of mystical-type experiences within the psychedelic literature (De Deus Pontual et al., 2023)-is most often indexed by its global score (Romeo et al., 2025), which averages across mystical experience, positive mood, transcendence of time/space, ineffability subscales.
text.formatted: For instance, the Mystical Experience Questionnaire (MEQ30; <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">MacLean et al., 2012)</ref>-one of the most commonly used measures of mystical-type experiences within the psychedelic literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(De Deus Pontual et al., 2023)</ref>-is most often indexed by its global score <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Romeo et al., 2025)</ref>, which averages across mystical experience, positive mood, transcendence of time/space, ineffability subscales.

text.text: While this total score and measures of 'complete mystical experience' have often shown robust associations with psychedelic-assisted therapy outcomes (Barrett et al., 2015; McCulloch et al., 2022; Romeo et al., 2025), the MEQ30's validated subscales, based on earlier phenomenological analysis of mystical reports across cultures and traditions (Stace, 1960), 1 are often overlooked.
text.formatted: While this total score and measures of 'complete mystical experience' have often shown robust associations with psychedelic-assisted therapy outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barrett et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">McCulloch et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Romeo et al., 2025)</ref>, the MEQ30's validated subscales, based on earlier phenomenological analysis of mystical reports across cultures and traditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Stace, 1960</ref>), 1 are often overlooked.

text.text: In addition to the MEQ30 global score combining multiple facets of experience, so too do its subscales.

For instance, the mystical experience subscale taps into experiences of insight, a sense of eternity, spiritual elevation, feelings of unity, heightened awareness, and transcendence from self-limitations.

Similarly, the 5 Dimension Altered State of Consciousness scale (5D-ASC, Studerus et al., 2010)-another commonly used measure of subjective experience in the psychedelic field-combines multiple facets of self-transcendent experience.
text.formatted: Similarly, the 5 Dimension Altered State of Consciousness scale <ref type="bibr">(5D-ASC, Studerus et al., 2010)</ref>-another commonly used measure of subjective experience in the psychedelic field-combines multiple facets of self-transcendent experience.

text.text: For instance, the experiences of unity subscale spans a sense of global oneness, oneness with one's surroundings, and with past/present/future, alongside a sense of touching eternity, and feeling that conflicts and contradictions dissolving.

The higher-order oceanic 1 Stace's (1960) argued that unity is central to mystical experience and distinguished two fundamental forms: extrovertive unity (perceiving an underlying unity within the external world) and introvertive unity (an ineffable experience of undifferentiated oneness involving dissolution of ego, subject-object distinctions, and sensory content).
text.formatted: The higher-order oceanic 1 <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Stace's (1960)</ref> argued that unity is central to mystical experience and distinguished two fundamental forms: extrovertive unity (perceiving an underlying unity within the external world) and introvertive unity (an ineffable experience of undifferentiated oneness involving dissolution of ego, subject-object distinctions, and sensory content).

text.text: The MEQ30 was designed to reflect these and related features, including nontemporal and nonspatial qualities, inner subjectivity (a sensed inner presence or reality in all things), a noetic quality, a sense of sacredness, ineffability, and paradoxicality.
boundlessness dimension, a mystical construct similar to the MEQ30 total score (Liechti et al., 2017), spans positively experienced depersonalization, experience of unity and deeply positive mood.
text.formatted: boundlessness dimension, a mystical construct similar to the MEQ30 total score <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Liechti et al., 2017)</ref>, spans positively experienced depersonalization, experience of unity and deeply positive mood.

text.text: Even narrower measures blend multiple dimensions of experience; for instance, the Ego Dissolution Inventory assesses distortions in the subjective sense of self alongside a sense of interconnectedness/oneness (Nour et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Even narrower measures blend multiple dimensions of experience; for instance, the Ego Dissolution Inventory assesses distortions in the subjective sense of self alongside a sense of interconnectedness/oneness <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Nour et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: While such blended measures of mystical-type experiences provide an important bigpicture overview of broad dimensions of experience, theory and empirical work suggest that self-transcendent experiences and feelings of unity are not unitary but encompass overlapping though dissociable facets (Garcia-Romeu et al., 2015; Yaden et al., 2017a).
text.formatted: While such blended measures of mystical-type experiences provide an important bigpicture overview of broad dimensions of experience, theory and empirical work suggest that self-transcendent experiences and feelings of unity are not unitary but encompass overlapping though dissociable facets <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Garcia-Romeu et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Yaden et al., 2017a)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, empirical research has found that that only certain states, those characterized by a 'mystical' quality, sense of connection, expansion or positive mood, are associated with beneficial outcomes, whereas experiences predominated by time and space distortions, ineffability, and small self-size or ego dissolution appear less so or not at all (Barrett et al., 2015; Kałużna et al., 2022; McCulloch et al., 2022; Tyson et al., 2022; Yaden, 2020a).
text.formatted: For instance, empirical research has found that that only certain states, those characterized by a 'mystical' quality, sense of connection, expansion or positive mood, are associated with beneficial outcomes, whereas experiences predominated by time and space distortions, ineffability, and small self-size or ego dissolution appear less so or not at all <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barrett et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Kałużna et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">McCulloch et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Tyson et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Yaden, 2020a)</ref>.

text.text: Based on a review of constructs with a self-transcendent experience component, Yaden and colleagues (2017) proposed a broad theoretical distinction between experiences characterized by an annihilational or 'self-loss' component-marked by loss or attenuation of a bounded sense of self-and those characterized by a relational or 'connection' quality-involving felt connection with others, humanity, or the world.
text.formatted: Based on a review of constructs with a self-transcendent experience component, <ref type="bibr">Yaden and colleagues (2017)</ref> proposed a broad theoretical distinction between experiences characterized by an annihilational or 'self-loss' component-marked by loss or attenuation of a bounded sense of self-and those characterized by a relational or 'connection' quality-involving felt connection with others, humanity, or the world.

text.text: Overall, while the emphasis on global, mystical-type experiences (e.g., MEQ30 total, 5D-ASC oceanic boundlessness) in psychedelic research may capture the often-blended nature of psychedelic experiences, it may also obscure meaningful phenomenological dimensions that are relevant for clinical change and for optimizing therapeutic context.

Although recent work has begun to elaborate theoretical frameworks for organizing types of self-transcendent and mystical experiences (Cova & Abatista, 2025; Stocker et al., 2024), a cohesive and widely accepted delineation and operationalization of self-transcendent experience types-and their differential relevance for therapeutic outcomes-remains lacking.
text.formatted: Although recent work has begun to elaborate theoretical frameworks for organizing types of self-transcendent and mystical experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Cova & Abatista, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Stocker et al., 2024)</ref>, a cohesive and widely accepted delineation and operationalization of self-transcendent experience types-and their differential relevance for therapeutic outcomes-remains lacking.

text.text: The current study sought to address this gap by clarifying higher-order dimensions of psychedelic-occasioned self-transcendent experiences and examining whether these distinctions have practical and psychological significance, with the goal of supporting more precise and conceptually parsimonious measurement.

To this end, we conducted an exploratory factor analysis to identify higher-order components of psychedelic-occasioned self-transcendent experiences across several measures relating to self-transcendent experiences and examined how these components relate to mindset at the time of substance ingestion, negative acute experiences, and persisting positive psychological effects.

The pre-registered secondary data analysis (https://osf.io/a4f9e) is part of a broader online observational study comparing mystical and self-transcendent experiences while under the influence of cannabis, MDMA and psilocybin.
text.formatted: The pre-registered secondary data analysis (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/a4f9e">https://osf.io/a4f9e</ref>) is part of a broader online observational study comparing mystical and self-transcendent experiences while under the influence of cannabis, MDMA and psilocybin.

text.text: Full study details and sample characteristics have previously been described (redacted-for-anonymous-review).
Briefly, 397 adult participants reported on an experience with cannabis (n = 131), MDMA (n = 133), or psilocybin (n = 133) in the past 5 years that was at least of a moderate subjective intensity.
In the present study, all analyses were run with the full sample given that substance type had a small impact on self-transcendent and related experiences (redacted-for-anonymizedreview).
Participants had a mean age of 34.3 years (SD = 9.5).
Gender was 60% men, 38% women, and 2% nonbinary.
The sample was 59% white, 29% Black or African American, 10% Hispanic or Latinx, 8% Asian, 1% Indigenous/American Indian, and 2% mixed race.
Data and associated code for the present study are available online (https://osf.io/ayjgh).
text.formatted: Data and associated code for the present study are available online (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/ayjgh">https://osf.io/ayjgh</ref>).

text.text: Study procedures were approved by the [redacted-for-anonymized-review] Institutional Review Board (redacted-for-anonymized-review) and carried out in accordance with the provisions of the World Medical Association Declaration of Helsinki.

Because the majority of the sample (83%) endorsed recreational purposes (redactedfor-anonymized-review), we created a binary variable coded as 1 for therapeutic or healing purposes (treating a mental or physical health condition, self-improvement, spiritual reasons, or deepening a connection) and 0 for non-healing or recreational purposes.
Supplementary Appendix A presents additional measures information.

Measures assessing intention and mindset at the time of substance ingestion that were identified as predictors of psychedelic-induced mystical experience in a systematic review were administered (Aday et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Measures assessing intention and mindset at the time of substance ingestion that were identified as predictors of psychedelic-induced mystical experience in a systematic review were administered <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Aday et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Five items assessed spiritual-prosocial motivations (Russ et al., 2019).

Negative emotions (upset, hostile, ashamed, nervous, afraid) during the substance use experience were assessed with the negative emotion subscale adapted from the International Positive and Negative Affect Schedule -Short Form (Thompson, 2007), a widely used measure of affective states that has shown good reliability and validity in diverse populations (Merz et al., 2013; Navarrete et al., 2025).

Persisting positive changes attributed to the substance use experience were assessed using four items adapted from the Persisting Effects Questionnaire-a commonly used approach to assess enduring positive and negative effects attributed to psychedelicoccasioned experiences (Griffiths et al., 2011 (Griffiths et al., , 2016 (Griffiths et al., , 2019;; McCulloch et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Persisting positive changes attributed to the substance use experience were assessed using four items adapted from the Persisting Effects Questionnaire-a commonly used approach to assess enduring positive and negative effects attributed to psychedelicoccasioned experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Griffiths et al., 2011</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Griffiths et al., , 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Griffiths et al., , 2019;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">McCulloch et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Participants were asked whether the experience or their contemplation of that experience has led to long-term and persisting changes in their: 'personal well-being or life satisfaction', 'life's purpose', 'mood' and 'behavioral changes.'
Items were averaged into a composite persisting positive effects score to reduce pairwise comparisons; internal consistency was excellent (α = .91).
Self-Transcendent Experiences.

The 9-item Self-Transcendent Experiences Survey (Yaden, 2020a) was included in the current study because it specifically assesses selftranscendent states without blending other related constructs (e.g., spiritual or religious experiences, noetic qualities).
text.formatted: The 9-item Self-Transcendent Experiences Survey <ref type="bibr">(Yaden, 2020a)</ref> was included in the current study because it specifically assesses selftranscendent states without blending other related constructs (e.g., spiritual or religious experiences, noetic qualities).

text.text: Five items assess self-loss self-transcendent experiences (sample item: "I felt my sense of self completely fade away"; α = .90 in the current study) and five assess connection self-transcendent experiences (sample item: "I had the sense of feeling closely connected to everything"; α = .94 in the current study) (Yaden, 2020a).
text.formatted: Five items assess self-loss self-transcendent experiences (sample item: "I felt my sense of self completely fade away"; α = .90 in the current study) and five assess connection self-transcendent experiences (sample item: "I had the sense of feeling closely connected to everything"; α = .94 in the current study) <ref type="bibr">(Yaden, 2020a)</ref>.

text.text: This scale has shown good convergent, discriminate and predictive validity in initial validation work (Yaden, 2020a).
text.formatted: This scale has shown good convergent, discriminate and predictive validity in initial validation work <ref type="bibr">(Yaden, 2020a)</ref>.

text.text: Five items adapted from the modified Differential Emotion Scale (Fredrickson et al., 2003b) were selected to assess the peak intensity of a range of self-transcendent emotions (awe, gratitude, inspiration, love, and sympathy) during the substance use experience.
text.formatted: Five items adapted from the modified Differential Emotion Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Fredrickson et al., 2003b)</ref> were selected to assess the peak intensity of a range of self-transcendent emotions (awe, gratitude, inspiration, love, and sympathy) during the substance use experience.

text.text: Items were intercorrelated (ρs: 0.52-.70, ps < .001) and averaged in the current study because a confirmatory factor analysis run using lavaan (Rosseel, 2012) supported a one-factor model of positive self-transcendent emotions (standardized factor loadings on the single latent factor: 0.77-0.89).
text.formatted: Items were intercorrelated (ρs: 0.52-.70, ps < .001) and averaged in the current study because a confirmatory factor analysis run using lavaan <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Rosseel, 2012)</ref> supported a one-factor model of positive self-transcendent emotions (standardized factor loadings on the single latent factor: 0.77-0.89).

text.text: Internal reliability was excellent in the current study (α = .90).
The Mystical Experiences Questionnaire (MEQ) was designed to assess various facets of mystical experiences that may result from hallucinogen use (MacLean et al., 2012).
text.formatted: The Mystical Experiences Questionnaire (MEQ) was designed to assess various facets of mystical experiences that may result from hallucinogen use <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(MacLean et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: We administered the widely-used 30-item version (MEQ30), which has demonstrated good reliability and construct validity in past work (Barrett et al., 2015; Wirsching et al., 2024).
text.formatted: We administered the widely-used 30-item version (MEQ30), which has demonstrated good reliability and construct validity in past work <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barrett et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Wirsching et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The MEQ30 has four subscales: transcendence of time and space (sample item: "Loss of your usual sense of time"), ineffability (sample item: "Sense that the experience cannot be described adequately in words"), positive mood (sample item "Experience of ecstasy"), and mystical experiences (sample item: "Gain of insightful knowledge experienced at an intuitive level").
These subscales and the total score demonstrated good internal reliability in the current study (αs = .84-.97).
Per convention (Griffiths et al., 2018), scores were calculated as a percentage of the maximum possible score, and thus could range from 0-100.

text.text: Self-Other Overlap.

The Inclusion of Other in the Self Scale (IOS; Aron et al., 1992) is a widely used single-item pictorial measure of interpersonal closeness, administered in the current study to assess self-other overlap.
text.formatted: The Inclusion of Other in the Self Scale (IOS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Aron et al., 1992)</ref> is a widely used single-item pictorial measure of interpersonal closeness, administered in the current study to assess self-other overlap.

text.text: This measure presents a series of Venn diagrams depicting increasing overlap between self/others; participants in the current study were asked to select the picture that best described "how connected you felt with other people during the experience."
Responses range from 1 (no overlap) to 7 (mostly overlapping), with a N/A (I was not with others) option available.

In its original validation study, the IOS demonstrated alternate-form and test-retest reliability, convergent validity and discriminant validity, and predictive validity for later relationship outcomes (Aron et al., 1992).

text.text: We conducted an exploratory factor analysis (EFA) using the ten scales or subscales (if a measure had subscales) described above: self-loss and connection self-transcendent experiences, self-transcendent emotions, MEQ30 subscales (transcendence of time and space, ineffability, positive mood, mystical experiences), small self (vastness and selfdiminishment), and self-other overlap.
Because measures were administered on distinct scales, variables were z-score standardized.
Best practices for EFA were followed when deciding upon extraction method, rotation method, and factor retention criteria (Goretzko et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Best practices for EFA were followed when deciding upon extraction method, rotation method, and factor retention criteria <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Goretzko et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: To determine the number of factors to retain, we examined the scree plot, conducted a parallel analysis, and examined factor loadings and overall variance explained by factor solutions.

A maximum likelihood EFA was run, with promax and oblim rotations compared on the basis of explained variance, theoretical parsimony of factor solution, and model fit indices (Tucker Lewis Index (TLI), RMSEA (Root Mean Square Error of Approximation) index, Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC)).
Indicators were then removed one-by-one from the factor analysis until a stable solution was identified.
First, indicators with very low communality scores (< .20) were removed (Costello & Osborne, 2005; Samuels, 2017).

text.text: Next, indicators were removed that most strongly violated the .40-.30-.20 rule (i.e., did not load onto primary factor above .40, the alternative factors below 0.30, or demonstrated a difference >0.20 between primary and alternative factor loadings) (Howard, 2016).

text.text: Once the final factor solution was determined, individual regression-based factor scores were calculated (McNeish & Wolf, 2020).

text.text: Zero-order correlations between factors and other study variables were examined; given that some variables showed skew, Spearman correlations were used.

We then ran a series of regression analyses with the regression-based factor scores together predicting various dependent measures: negative emotions (Model 1), positive persisting effects (Model 2), state of surrender (Model 3), apprehensiveness at time of substance ingestion (Model 4), clarity of intentions (Model 5), spiritual-prosocial motivations (Model 6), and primary purpose for use (Model 7).
Across models, multicollinearity was not observed (VIF values < 2).
text.formatted: Across models, multicollinearity was not observed (VIF values < 2).

text.text: For Model 4, an ordinal regression was used.
For Model 7, a binomial logistic regression was used.
For the remainder of the models, which had continuous dependent measures, linear regression assumptions were tested.
Across models, some heteroscedasticity was observed; as such, robust standard errors were used.

For models in which the assumption of normality of residuals was violated (per examination of diagnostic plots), generalized linear models (negative binomial, gamma, Tweedie) were tested for improved model fit.
For Model 1, a negative binomial model best fit the data.
For Models 2, 3, and 5, linear regressions best fit the data.
For linear regression models, adjusted R² values are presented; for other models, McFadden pseudo R² was calculated with the pscl package (Jackman et al., 2015).

text.text: Supplementary Appendix B presents correlations between study variables.
The scree plot and parallel analysis suggested that a 1-2 factor solution may best fit the data.
Both were tested and compared, with a two-factor solution with oblimin rotation selected due to significant model fit improvements and greater theoretical parsimony.
Supplementary Appendix C presents the scree plot, parallel analysis, and details on the selection of a twofactor solution.
The small self-self-diminishment item was removed first from the EFA because it showed low communality (h² = .14), indicating little variance explained by the factor solution.
Next, the mystical experiences subscale was removed from the EFA due to high loading on the alternative factor (0.64 on the primary factor, and 0.40 on secondary).
Finally, the vastness relative to the self-subscale was removed due to low discrepancy in factor loadings between the primary and secondary factor (0.51 and 0.34, respectively).
The final two-factor solution explained 67% of the total variance (37% for Factor 1 and 30% for Factor 2) and demonstrated good fit (RMSEA index = 0.09, TLI = 0.96, BIC = -11.63).

text.text: The first factor was comprised of the connection self-transcendence, mystical experiences, self-transcendent emotions, and inclusion of self in other subscales and accounted for 35% of the total variance.
This factor was consequently named "Connection and Positive Emotions."
The second factor was comprised of the self-loss self-transcendence, transcendence of time and space, and ineffability subscales, and accounted for 32% total variance.
This factor was consequently named "Time, Space and Self-Transcendence."
The extracted factors were moderately intercorrelated (Spearman rho = .62, p < .001).

text.text: The present study sought to clarify the higher-order organization of psychedelicoccasioned self-transcendent experiences, and to examine whether these distinctions show meaningful associations with mindset, acute affective responses, and persisting positive effects.

Drawing on measures of self-transcendent experience, self-transcendent emotion, mystical-type experience, small self, and self-other overlap, an exploratory factor analysis yielded two correlated but distinct components.

One factor, labelled Connection and Positive Emotions, was characterized by connection-oriented self-transcendent experiences, selftranscendent and positive emotions, and greater inclusion of others in the self.

The second factor, labelled Time, Space, and Self-Transcendence, reflected elements of self-transcendent experience characterized by loss of sense of self, distortions of time and space, and ineffability.

These components showed distinct patterns of associations with outcomes-with only the Connection and Positive Emotions factor corresponding to beneficial outcomesunderscoring the importance of fine-grained assessment to differentiate between qualitatively distinct forms of self-transcendent experiences.

Both factors of self-transcendent experiences were moderately-to-strongly intercorrelated (ρ = .65), consistent with the blended phenomenology of subjective psychedelic experiences having a "common core" (MacLean et al., 2012; Stace, 1960; Watts et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Both factors of self-transcendent experiences were moderately-to-strongly intercorrelated (ρ = .65), consistent with the blended phenomenology of subjective psychedelic experiences having a "common core" <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(MacLean et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Stace, 1960;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Watts et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, psychedelic experiences often appear to involve both a loosening of self-boundaries and an enhanced sense of affective connection and unity.
Yet, the factors showed differential relations with affective responses during the experience and with persisting positive outcomes.

This pattern aligns with theoretical perspectives proposing that self-transcendent/mystical experiences are multifaceted, comprising interrelated yet separable components (Cova & Seragnoli, 2025; Wittmann, 2015; Yaden et al., 2017b), as well as with prior empirical work demonstrating that self-transcendent experiences characterized by selfloss versus connection show distinct associations (Cova & Abatista, 2025; Yaden, 2020a).

text.text: Broad total scores assessing wide-ranging constructs (e.g., mystical-type experiences, oceanic boundlessness) provide a useful, big-picture overview of psychedelic effects; however, they can obscure fine-grained distinctions among experiential facets and may limit the field's ability to link specific phenomenological components to distinct mechanisms of action and therapeutic levers if not used in tandem with other granular assessment (Yaden et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Broad total scores assessing wide-ranging constructs (e.g., mystical-type experiences, oceanic boundlessness) provide a useful, big-picture overview of psychedelic effects; however, they can obscure fine-grained distinctions among experiential facets and may limit the field's ability to link specific phenomenological components to distinct mechanisms of action and therapeutic levers if not used in tandem with other granular assessment <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Yaden et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: We recommend that assessments of altered states include not only total scores but also subscale-level information, supplemented by targeted measures of theorized mechanisms of change (e.g., connectedness, Davis et al., 2021; psychological insight, Watts et al., 2022; awe, Yaden et al., 2018; self-transcendent emotion, Fredrickson et al., 2003a).
text.formatted: We recommend that assessments of altered states include not only total scores but also subscale-level information, supplemented by targeted measures of theorized mechanisms of change (e.g., connectedness, <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Davis et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">psychological insight, Watts et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">awe, Yaden et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">self-transcendent emotion, Fredrickson et al., 2003a)</ref>.

text.text: Supporting this recommendation, research has found that the explanatory power of the MEQ30 is increased when other dimensions-connectedness, paradoxicality-are added (Stocker et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Supporting this recommendation, research has found that the explanatory power of the MEQ30 is increased when other dimensions-connectedness, paradoxicality-are added <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Stocker et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, findings suggest that integrating granular assessments of specific facets of altered and self-transcendent experiences with traditional mystical measures may better isolate the phenomenological elements most relevant to enduring clinical change.

The Connection and Positive Emotions factor identified in this study overlaps with several other constructs delineated in past empirical and conceptual work, including the relational or connection component of self-transcendent experiences (Yaden, 2020b; Yaden et al., 2017b), the vastness component of small self and awe, in which one feels a part of something grand, powerful, or greater than oneself (Tyson et al., 2022; Yaden et al., 2018), connectedness to self, others and the world (Watts et al., 2022), and "extroverted mysticism" or a sense of unity with the external world (Stace, 1960).
text.formatted: The Connection and Positive Emotions factor identified in this study overlaps with several other constructs delineated in past empirical and conceptual work, including the relational or connection component of self-transcendent experiences <ref type="bibr">(Yaden, 2020b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Yaden et al., 2017b)</ref>, the vastness component of small self and awe, in which one feels a part of something grand, powerful, or greater than oneself <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Tyson et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Yaden et al., 2018)</ref>, connectedness to self, others and the world <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Watts et al., 2022)</ref>, and "extroverted mysticism" or a sense of unity with the external world <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Stace, 1960)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, the Connection and Positive Emotions factor integrates this relational-unitive quality with an explicitly affective dimension: overall positive emotions (e.g., bliss, peace) and self-transcendent emotions (awe, gratitude, inspiration, love, and sympathy).
Positive emotions and self-transcendent emotions are often measured separately from experiences of interconnectedness (Fredrickson et al., 2003a; Gordon et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Positive emotions and self-transcendent emotions are often measured separately from experiences of interconnectedness <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Fredrickson et al., 2003a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Gordon et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: However, self-transcendent emotions are closely theoretically linked to relational experiences, such as through reducing self-focus, fostering a sense of common humanity, and promoting prosocial concern for others and the world (Gordon et al., 2017).
text.formatted: However, self-transcendent emotions are closely theoretically linked to relational experiences, such as through reducing self-focus, fostering a sense of common humanity, and promoting prosocial concern for others and the world <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Gordon et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, awe may entail a sense of self-expansion, self-diminishment or connectedness (Yaden et al., 2018), gratitude supports relational health (Algoe et al., 2013) and love/compassion increase warmth, affiliation and bonding (Förster & Kanske, 2022).
text.formatted: For instance, awe may entail a sense of self-expansion, self-diminishment or connectedness <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Yaden et al., 2018)</ref>, gratitude supports relational health <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Algoe et al., 2013)</ref> and love/compassion increase warmth, affiliation and bonding <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Förster & Kanske, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: While positive emotions that are not explicitly self-transcendent are less directly tied to experiences of unity, they may nevertheless support feelings of connection by broadening attention and fostering interpersonal openness (Fredrickson, 2013).
text.formatted: While positive emotions that are not explicitly self-transcendent are less directly tied to experiences of unity, they may nevertheless support feelings of connection by broadening attention and fostering interpersonal openness <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Fredrickson, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: That connection and positive and self-transcendent emotions loaded together in the current study suggests that such emotions may be part of the experiential "blueprint" of altered states characterized by a sense of interconnectedness, and that treating them as entirely distinct may underrepresent how these experiences are lived.

Our work aligns with recent work postulating that self-transcendent emotions are central to psychedelic-induced experiences (Cova & Seragnoli, 2025), as well as finding that everyday experiences of unity are characterized by the presence of social emotions, such as compassion and love (Cova & Abatista, 2025), whereas these emotions were less characteristic of self-loss experiences.
text.formatted: Our work aligns with recent work postulating that self-transcendent emotions are central to psychedelic-induced experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Cova & Seragnoli, 2025)</ref>, as well as finding that everyday experiences of unity are characterized by the presence of social emotions, such as compassion and love <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Cova & Abatista, 2025)</ref>, whereas these emotions were less characteristic of self-loss experiences.

text.text: It's important to note that contemplative and philosophical accounts highlight that experiences of interconnection can be accompanied not only by bliss and compassion, but also by contact with suffering.
For instance, Thich Nhat Hanh's description of "interbeing" captures how a deep sense of shared existence can expose one to others' pain as well as their joy (e.g., "If you suffer, I suffer.
If you are not safe, I am not safe") (Hanh, 2017).
text.formatted: If you are not safe, I am not safe") <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Hanh, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The present study did not include such dimensions in the factor analysis; future work could examine how connection, positive emotion, and painful affect co-occur within selftranscendent experiences.

The Time, Space, and Self-Transcendence factor identified in the present study overlaps with constructs delineated in past empirical and conceptual work, such as descriptions of dissolving temporal and spatial boundaries and ineffability during psychedelic states (MacLean et al., 2012), the annihilational or self-loss component of self-transcendent experiences (Yaden, 2020b; Yaden et al., 2017b), and ego dissolution (though this construct also blends feelings of oneness/connection) (Nour et al., 2016).
text.formatted: The Time, Space, and Self-Transcendence factor identified in the present study overlaps with constructs delineated in past empirical and conceptual work, such as descriptions of dissolving temporal and spatial boundaries and ineffability during psychedelic states <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(MacLean et al., 2012)</ref>, the annihilational or self-loss component of self-transcendent experiences <ref type="bibr">(Yaden, 2020b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Yaden et al., 2017b)</ref>, and ego dissolution (though this construct also blends feelings of oneness/connection) <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Nour et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This factor aligns closely with the concept of "introverted mysticism," described as an ineffable experience of undifferentiated unity that involves the complete dissolution of the ego, subject-object distinctions and sensory content (Stace, 1960).
text.formatted: This factor aligns closely with the concept of "introverted mysticism," described as an ineffable experience of undifferentiated unity that involves the complete dissolution of the ego, subject-object distinctions and sensory content <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Stace, 1960)</ref>.

text.text: Our work also aligns with research in time perception; for instance, Wittman describes how bodily states (affective, interoceptive) are inherently intertwined with time perception, such that diminished bodily awareness and selfreferential processing can contribute to feelings of timelessness (Wittmann, 2015).
text.formatted: Our work also aligns with research in time perception; for instance, Wittman describes how bodily states (affective, interoceptive) are inherently intertwined with time perception, such that diminished bodily awareness and selfreferential processing can contribute to feelings of timelessness <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Wittmann, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with these conceptualizations, our findings suggest that dissolutions of time, space, and self tend to co-occur, representing a unified perceptual-cognitive process in which the usual anchor points from which human experience is referenced fade together.

This co-occurrence aligns with recent findings from Cova & Abatista (2025) in which everyday experiences characterized by a sense of self-loss were associated with disruptions in the perception of space and time to a greater degree than experiences characterized by a sense of unity/connection.
text.formatted: This co-occurrence aligns with recent findings from <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Cova & Abatista (2025)</ref> in which everyday experiences characterized by a sense of self-loss were associated with disruptions in the perception of space and time to a greater degree than experiences characterized by a sense of unity/connection.

text.text: Of note, the co-occurrence of time, space and self-dissolution contrasts with Yaden and colleagues' (2017) premise that relational self-transcendent experiences, versus self-loss self-transcendent experiences, may encompass spatial unity, based upon theories linking social and spatial unity (Parkinson et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Of note, the co-occurrence of time, space and self-dissolution contrasts with <ref type="bibr">Yaden and colleagues' (2017)</ref> premise that relational self-transcendent experiences, versus self-loss self-transcendent experiences, may encompass spatial unity, based upon theories linking social and spatial unity <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Parkinson et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Both components of self-transcendent experiences were robustly associated with aspects of intention and mindset at the time of substance ingestion.

Connection and Positive Emotions showed consistent associations with greater spiritual-prosocial motivations, higher clarity of intentions, greater state of surrender, greater likelihood of having had a primarily therapeutic/healing purpose for use, as well as lower apprehensiveness at time of ingestion.

While Time, Space, and Self-Transcendence was similarly positively linked with spiritualprosocial motivations and surrender, it was associated with greater apprehensiveness at time of ingestion, with a lower likelihood of having used the substance for therapeutic/healing purposes and had a small nonsignificant association with clarity of intentions.

These patterns suggest that spiritual or prosocial orientations and a stance of surrender may set the stage for both forms of self-transcendent experiences, whereas therapeutic/healing intentions for use, lower initial apprehensiveness, and to a lesser extent, clarity of intentions, may be especially conducive to affectively positive and connection-laden experiences.

From a therapeutic standpoint, careful preparation around apprehension and fear-normalizing challenging experiences and helping clients relate differently to them-may be particularly important when aiming to facilitate self-transcendent experiences involving a sense of positive emotion and connection.
The two factors also showed distinct relationships with affect during the experience and persisting positive effects afterwards.
Connection and Positive Emotions was associated with fewer negative emotions acutely and with greater self-reported positive persisting effects.
In contrast, Time, Space, and Self-Transcendence predicted more intense negative emotions during the experience and was not associated with positive persisting effects.

This overall pattern aligns with empirical work finding that experiences characterized by a mystical quality, sense of connection, expansion or positive mood are associated with beneficial outcomes, whereas experiences predominantly characterized by a loss of sense of self, time and space, ineffability, and small self-size are not (Barrett et al., 2015; Cova & Abatista, 2025; McCulloch et al., 2022; Tyson et al., 2022; Yaden, 2020a).
